title: Optimal harvest planning in uneven-aged stands: balancing post-treatment seed arrival with seedling establishment
content:
Abstract
Harvest planning in uneven-aged stands is challenging in ecosystems where operational success depends on uncertain recruitment dynamics. Conventional management practices, designed to maintain a target diameter distribution, overlook the ecological processes driving post-harvest regeneration. We present a proof-of-concept framework that optimizes tree-level harvest decisions based on their predicted effects on seed arrival and seedling establishment. The study focuses on a low-elevation, uneven-aged European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.) stand growing in a drought-prone Mediterranean region. We hypothesized that harvest intensity and tree selection emerge from jointly modelling the dual role of mature trees as seed sources and competitors of seedlings. Seed dispersal was monitored over 2023–5 using 43 seed traps, while seedling recruitment was surveyed in 2025 across 124 quadrats. An objective function was developed to quantify the effects of tree harvesting on recruitment, integrating two models that link adult basal area with predicted seed and seedling counts. A genetic algorithm was then used to identify a harvest plan maximizing the post-harvest objective function score. A classical BDq harvest plan was also developed as a benchmark. This approach defines a target diameter distribution and identifies trees for removal as surplus stems relative to that target distribution. Results show that the new framework reduces the initial basal area by 21.8% (from 22.5 to 17.6 m2·ha−1) and achieves an 11.9% increase in the post-harvest objective function score relative to the pre-harvest baseline, whereas the BDq plan resulted in a 6% decrease. Notably, the optimization converged to an operationally realistic harvest intensity without prescribing a target residual basal area or harvest intensity. Model-based predictions indicate that, if implemented, the optimized harvest plan would increase seedling abundance across 60.2% of the stand area (comprising 41.2% without predicted seed loss and 19.0% with seed loss), while the rest would remain unaffected by harvesting. In our suggested framework, a tree is selected for harvest when the reduction in seed arrival caused by its removal is outweighed by the gain in recruitment potential from released growing space, allowing harvest intensity to emerge directly from optimization rather than from a predefined structural target. This study introduces the first tree-level harvest-planning framework explicitly grounded in recruitment processes for uneven-aged stands. As a proof of concept, the framework demonstrates the feasibility of this approach; however, its model-based predictions require validation through field implementation before operational use.
